questions.question: Explain how the mineral revolution led to the South African War and what the Peace of Vereeniging decided.
questions.expected_answer: After 1886 the richest gold fields in the world lay in the Transvaal, an independent Boer republic. The industry was owned mainly by British and foreign investors, and Britain wanted the gold fields inside a British-controlled South Africa; disputes over taxes, the dynamite concession and the vote for uitlanders, and the failed Jameson Raid of 1895 to 1896, increased tension. War broke out in October 1899. After the fall of the Boer capitals, Boer commandos fought a guerrilla war, and Britain used scorched earth and concentration camps, where about 26 000 to 28 000 Boer women and children and at least 14 000, probably over 20 000, black people died. The Peace of Vereeniging of 31 May 1902 made the Transvaal and the Orange Free State British colonies, promised self-government and reconstruction money, and postponed the question of the vote for black people until after self-government, which meant that white voters would decide.

questions.question: Describe how coloured, Indian and African South Africans organised and resisted between 1902 and 1910.
questions.expected_answer: Coloured people in Cape Town formed the African Political Organisation in 1902, led from 1905 by Dr Abdullah Abdurahman; it defended the Cape franchise and sought equal rights in the north through petitions, a newspaper and delegations. Indians in the Transvaal formed the Transvaal British Indian Association in 1903, later the Transvaal Indian Congress, and in 1906 Gandhi and the community pledged to refuse to obey a law forcing Indian men to register with fingerprints, beginning satyagraha, peaceful refusal to obey unjust laws. Africans published newspapers such as Imvo Zabantsundu and Ilanga lase Natal and formed regional congresses. In Natal, resistance to the poll tax of 1905 led to the Bambatha Rebellion of 1906, crushed at the Mome Gorge with three to four thousand Africans killed. In 1909 a delegation including Schreiner, Abdurahman and Jabavu protested in London against the draft constitution.

questions.question: Explain why the Union of South Africa in 1910 is seen as a turning point in the balance of power.
questions.expected_answer: The Union joined the Cape, Natal, the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony into one state on 31 May 1910, under the South Africa Act of 1909 drawn up by an all-white National Convention, with Louis Botha as Prime Minister. Only white men could be elected to Parliament; the Cape kept its qualified non-racial franchise, but in the other provinces only white men voted. In 1911 white people were about 21 per cent of the population, roughly one in five, but held almost all political power. By 1910 the African kingdoms had been defeated and the Boer republics conquered, so the whole region apart from the protectorates was united under a white minority government with an economy based on mining and migrant labour, which shaped South African history for most of the twentieth century.
